title: Towards the development of a national drought monitoring framework for India: Reconstruction of historical droughts using CLM5
abstract: Abstract. In this study, we evaluate the Community Land Model version 5.0 (CLM5.0) as a first step toward building a National Drought Monitoring Framework – DRISHTI (Drought Risk &amp; Impact Surveillance using Hydrometeorological, Terrestrial &amp; Inference Models) in India. CLM5.0 was applied over India at 0.1 ° resolution (1980–2020), using India Meteorological Department (IMD) precipitation and two atmospheric forcing datasets: the Indian Monsoon Data Assimilation and Analysis (IMDAA) regional reanalysis and the fifth generation ECMWF Re-Analysis (ERA5). Model performance was assessed for soil moisture (SM), evapotranspiration (ET), and runoff under rainfed and irrigated conditions against in-situ measurements and satellite/reference datasets: Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP), Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM), and Global Runoff Reconstruction (GRUN). CLM5.0 reproduced spatial and temporal hydrological variability well. Model diagnostics revealed three climate-zone biases: (1) an apparent 'Dry Bias' in humid zones (Am) characterized by low SM, runoff, and ET. This bias reflects underestimation of precipitation in IMD rather than model process deficiencies; (2) a 'Wet Bias' in semi-arid and arid zones (BSh, BWh), where the Dry Surface Layer scheme suppresses evaporation, generating excess storage and runoff; and (3) a 'Runoff Paradox' in temperate zones (Cwa, Cwb), where high surface SM coincides with low runoff. Systematic runoff underestimation in complex terrains reflects limitations in sub-grid hillslope lateral flow representation, which led to high moisture retention. Relative to ERA5-driven simulations, IMDAA reduces RMSD in SM and runoff by 10% and 2.5 %, respectively, while ERA5 improves ET estimates by 17 %. At the national scale, rainfed simulations generally outperform irrigated runs; however, irrigation leads to localized improvements - most notably over the Indo-Gangetic Plain - with a stronger influence on root-zone SM than on surface SM. Specifically, irrigation reduces errors over ~26 % of irrigated grid cells for root-zone SM compared to ~23 % for surface SM, while corresponding improvements are observed over ~33 % and ~45 % of irrigated grid cells for runoff and ET, respectively. Despite these limitations, CLM5.0 successfully reproduces historical droughts, demonstrating its utility for drought monitoring in data-scarce regions while highlighting the need for improved irrigation parameterization, targeted model calibration, and careful selection of meteorological forcing datasets.
problem: The development of a national drought monitoring framework for India is hindered by sparse in-situ data and the unevaluated performance of advanced land surface models in accurately simulating key hydrological variables across the country's diverse and heavily irrigated landscapes.
method: This study evaluates the Community Land Model 5.0 (CLM5) to reconstruct historical droughts for a monitoring framework in India by simulating hydrological variables under different atmospheric forcings and comparing outputs against in-situ, satellite, and reanalysis datasets.
task: The task is to evaluate the Community Land Model version 5.0 (CLM5) for its ability to reconstruct historical droughts and simulate key hydrological variables across India, as a foundational step toward developing a national drought monitoring framework.

In CLM5.0, soil thickness ranges from 0 to 8.5 meters, divided into 20 hydrologically active layers, with increasing depth from top to bottom.

Atmospheric forcing strongly controls hydrological partitioning: IMDAA forcing reduces soil moisture and runoff RMSD by 10% and 2.5%, respectively, whereas ERA5 reduces evapotranspiration RMSD by 17%.

SMAP, launched in 2015, was the first mission dedicated to SM and freeze/thaw monitoring using both radar and radiometer at L-band, the radar component ceased functioning after three months, leaving only the passive radiometer operational (Entekhabi et al., 2010).

The Indian Cosmic Ray Network (ICON) operates the Cosmic-ray Soil Moisture Observation System (COSMOS) at seven sites across India (Upadhyaya et al., 2021). In this study, SM data from three locations: Berampudi (BMB), Madahalli (MDH), and Singanallur (SGR) - were used to evaluate the model's performance in simulating SM.

To assess CLM5's capability in simulating historical droughts, this study reconstructs major meteorological and agricultural monsoon droughts from 1987, 2002, 2009, and 2015, and hydrological droughts during the 2018 monsoon and the 2003 and 2016 water years, based on prior studies (Chuphal et al., 2024; Mishra, 2020; Mishra et al., 2018). For the drought analysis, all land-surface variables (SM, ET, and runoff) are taken from the IMDAA-Rfd configuration. This setup was selected because it provides the best overall hydrological consistency, reducing RMSD for SM (10%) and runoff (2.5%) relative to ERA5-Rfd, despite exhibiting higher ET errors (by 17%) compared with ERA5-based simulations.

To evaluate meteorological, agricultural, and hydrological droughts, we used three standardized indices: the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010), the Standardised Soil Moisture Index (SSI; Hao & AghaKouchak, 2013), and Standardized Runoff Index (SRI; Shukla & Wood, 2008), respectively.
The BSh zone covers the drier regions of Western and Southern India, with low to moderate rainfall, while the Thar Desert, part of the BWh zone, experiences very low rainfall.

The Cwa and Cwb zones, covering central, northeastern, and eastern India, including parts of the Ganga and Brahmaputra basins, form extensive agricultural regions with moderate to heavy rainfall (Upadhyaya and Ramsankaran, 2018).
